sourceTitle: The Tyranny of the Blue Ticks
scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Ten independent interpretation, argument and critical-transfer questions, pending teacher review.

questions.q: What new social meaning do read receipts attach to opening a message?
choices: Reading can be mistaken for a commitment to answer promptly.
They confirm the sender understood the message correctly.
They prevent the receiver from ignoring unwanted requests.
They show exactly when the reader has free time.
questions.explanation: The writer describes opening a message as a promise from the sender's perspective.

questions.q: Why is the café worker an example of unequal communication pressure?
choices: Every worker has an identical chance to accept a shift.
Fast replies bring rewards unavailable to people who are offline.
The manager formally orders workers to stay online.
Workers must answer only during their contracted hours.
questions.explanation: The informal system rewards whoever is available immediately, regardless of circumstances.

questions.q: Which important distinction cannot a read receipt make?
choices: Whether the message has been opened at all.
Whether an emergency message is sent to the right number.
Whether the reader is also in a position to respond.
Whether both participants use the same application.
questions.explanation: The author separates seeing a message from having the time or resources to answer it.

questions.q: Why does the writer concede that receipts can be useful in an emergency?
choices: To suggest that all messages should be treated as urgent.
To establish that every delay is intentionally disrespectful.
To argue that employers should monitor private reading.
To acknowledge a legitimate benefit before showing the feature's limits.
questions.explanation: The qualified concession makes the criticism more balanced.

questions.q: Why do groups' unspoken expectations create indirect conflict?
choices: Every group has written and consistently enforced rules.
Members may follow different rules without knowing they disagree.
Longer delays always mean a lack of commitment.
Emojis reliably resolve every disagreement about tone.
questions.explanation: The author links invisible norms to misread delays and passive-aggressive responses.

questions.q: What is the point of comparing a school club with the right to disconnect?
choices: School clubs must apply employment law directly.
The author wants friends to replace all work messages.
Only countries with such laws can agree on response times.
Explicit boundaries can protect free time in formal and informal groups.
questions.explanation: The article transfers the principle of agreed communication limits to small groups.

questions.q: A staff chat grants extra shifts to whoever replies at midnight first. What should a fair manager reconsider?
choices: Whether the system unfairly rewards constant availability.
Whether the fastest responders write grammatically correct texts.
Whether late-night messages are more honest.
Whether the chat should use brighter notification colours.
questions.explanation: The example demonstrates unequal access and pressure despite no explicit order.

questions.q: Someone turns off read receipts and their friends see that as rejection. What is the relevant lesson?
choices: Turning off receipts always means a friendship is ending.
The app can guarantee that no one interprets the choice.
Technical choices can carry social meanings that users cannot fully control.
Friends should be legally required to leave receipts on.
questions.explanation: The author challenges the claim that switching off is a socially neutral option.

questions.q: A newcomer is unsure whether a delayed reply offends a team. What would best address the problem?
choices: Answer every message immediately, even at night.
Agree openly on expected response times instead of guessing.
Avoid asking because the rule should be obvious.
Send increasingly cheerful emojis to test reactions.
questions.explanation: The problem is not merely timing but the absence of stated shared norms.

questions.q: A friend sees two blue ticks but no reply. Which conclusion is most consistent with the essay?
choices: The friendship is now less important to the reader.
The reader is deliberately refusing all communication.
A prompt reply is therefore guaranteed tomorrow.
The message was seen; the person's level of care remains unknown.
questions.explanation: The final sentence warns against turning evidence of reading into a moral judgement.
